item.title: CoreWeave stock wipeout exposes divide between AI fear and greed
item.description: CoreWeave Inc. is navigating turbulent stock trends due to climbing bond yields and investor trepidation over its debt, raising fears of default. Although a temporary boost followed optimistic comments from Nvidia's CEO, the overall sentiment leans towards caution. Analysts believe that while funding needs are pressing, robust AI demand could mitigate rate worries. Furthermore, CoreWeave's alliance with Nvidia may be a vital source of financial support in these unpredictable conditions.
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: CoreWeave Inc. has become caught in a tug of war between investors who see rising bond yields as a potential rally killer for the AI trade and those who think demand for computing power will make those concerns seem passe before long.The cloud-computing services provider’s shares plunged 20% in the first three sessions of the week, including more than 15% on Wednesday, as its debt tumbled to levels that typically indicate distress. On Thursday morning, the cost of protecting CoreWeave bonds against default rose to the highest intraday level on record, while swaps priced in a more than 60% chance of a default within the next five years.But by Thursday afternoon, the sense of panic appeared to be alleviating as the stock bounced into the green with Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia Corp., which is a CoreWeave shareholder and supplier, expressing confidence in the company. In addition, Deutsche Bank called the selloff a “buying opportunity.” The shares ended the day up 5.9%, their best performance in over a month.On Friday, the stock fell as much as 9.4% and is on track for a weekly drop of more than 20%, its biggest since November.134998814“The macro backdrop has created a sell-first, ask-questions-later market,” said Thomas DiFazio, exchange-traded fund strategist at Roundhill Financial. “In the short run, it is hard to say with a straight face that the all-clear is here.”As a so-called neocloud provider, Coreweave is at the heart of the infrastructure buildout needed to develop artificial intelligence technology. The safety of its debt is a key issue for investors because its spending on building data centers is being funded by issuing bonds. With Treasury yields climbing and inflation remaining stubbornly high, the cost of that financing is rising fast.Also Read: Global hedge funds suffer steep losses as AI trade unwinds, Asia funds hit hardestAll of which has led to a bumpy ride for CoreWeave shares. The stock is up more than 50% since its troubled initial public offering in March 2025 that had to be backstopped by Nvidia. But it’s down 12% this year and 66% since hitting a peak in June 2025, and it’s less than $30 from its debut price.However, the upside for CoreWeave is pretty obvious, as demand for AI computing services continues to outstrip supply. And there are few signs that dynamic is going to change any time soon, DiFazio said.That was the view taken by Deutsche Bank analyst Brad Zelnick, who has a buy rating on the stock and is urging investors to snap up the shares before they fully rebound.CoreWeave has “a strong customer base, established record of execution, backlog conversion and leading infrastructure performance,” Zelnick wrote in a research note on Thursday. “While more capital will be needed, this can happen at a steady pace and is backed by robust customer backlog.”Of course, CoreWeave wasn’t alone in this week’s selloff. The Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index, known by its ticker SOX, has dropped 9.7% this week, leaving it down 22% from a June peak. Server makers Dell Technologies Inc. and Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. have both fallen sharply.But CoreWeave is considered one of the riskiest stocks in the AI trade because of its heavy reliance on high-yield debt to finance its data centers. The company secured investment-grade ratings for its chip-backed debt for the first time in March and the goal is to keep winning similar ratings, co-founder Brannin McBee told the Financial Times on Wednesday, which just underscores how much more CoreWeave plans to borrow. The company’s close relationship with Nvidia could provide a source of capital if its market access tightens, according to Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Robert Schiffman. But Huang pushed back against that idea on Thursday, saying there’s no need for a bailout. “CoreWeave’s strength is improving every day,” Huang told Bloomberg at an event in Stockholm. “I’m optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing.”Still, even with all the risks posed by higher interest rates and the stratospheric level of AI spending, the fundamental backdrop remains encouraging for CoreWeave, according to Matt Bartolini, global head of research strategists for State Street Investment Management. “We’re still very early on in the AI capex cycle, so I don’t think rates will be the barrier that’s hard to jump over, but it does change the calculus behind the continued issuance of debt, and ensuring whether the financing of that debt can be met with credible growth in the future,” Bartolini said. “The secular demand story is what’s funding the capex cycle, and I think demand is likely to continue irrespective of what’s happening with rates.”

item.title: From worst to best: How IT stocks staged a Rs 2.6 lakh crore revival this week
item.description: Indian IT stocks staged a sharp comeback this week, adding Rs 2.6 lakh crore in market value as the sector gained 12% to become the best-performing index. Better-than-expected Q2 earnings, positive management commentary and a selloff in AI-linked stocks helped revive sentiment, even as concerns over AI adoption and earnings growth persist.
item.dc:creator: Veer Sharma
item.content:encoded: Market narratives can change quickly, and this week's performance of IT stocks is a case in point. Improved earnings and a downturn in AI-linked stocks, amid multi-billion-dollar investments failing to generate the returns stakeholders had hoped for, have helped IT stocks add Rs 2.60 lakh crore in market value. The index has risen 12%, making it the best-performing index this week.For the week, Tech Mahindra led the index with a gain of over 16%, followed by Wipro at 13%. TCS, Infosys and HCL Tech each advanced 12%. The rally is significant given that FIIs and other investors had fled IT stocks earlier this year as AI-linked stocks gained momentum amid heightened concerns over slowing demand and earnings.What helped IT flip the script?1.) AI’s $1 trillion plunge - US stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade fell on Thursday, extending a global sell-off that has wiped out more than $1 trillion in market value from 20 of the world's most valuable AI and semiconductor companies so far this week. Concerns over interest rate hikes, AI financing and intensifying competition weighed on investor sentiment.Tensions flared further after OpenAI told investors last week that its annualised revenue for September was nearly $50 billion, lower than the figure it had indicated earlier, Reuters reported. At a separate event, the company had previously told investors that its September revenue run rate was approaching $70 billion.2.) Q2 earnings come at an opportune time - IT companies have posted better-than-expected earnings. India’s largest player TCS reported 15% year-on-year (YoY) growth in its consolidated net profit at Rs 13,884 crore for the second quarter. The same stood at Rs 12,075 crore a year ago. The Board has declared a second interim dividend of Rs 12 per share for the financial year 2026-27.In constant currency terms, revenue rose 0.5% quarter-on-quarter. Operating margin came in at 24%, while net margin stood at 19%. CEO and MD K Krithivasan said the company saw broad-based growth across international markets and most industry segments.3.) Global giant Accenture forecast growth - At investor day, Accenture’s Chief Executive Officer Julie Sweet pushed to dispel fears that new technology poses a major threat to the consulting industry.“The opportunity is bigger than ever before,” she said. “While AI does have the potential, with AI efficiencies, to impact our business more than ever before, we again believe that ultimately, the new demand that will be created, will far exceed the demand that’s being replaced.” Accenture's commentary is closely watched as an indicator of global demand for technology services.4.) AI’s capital roadblock - Earlier this week, Broadcom’s Hock Tan said capital could become a bigger constraint on AI expansion than shortages of semiconductors, memory chips or electricity. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan echoed the concern, flagging the rising cost of capital and the need for companies investing heavily in AI to demonstrate adequate returns.The warnings come as investors reassess the sustainability of the AI-driven rally amid stretched valuations, intensifying competition and uncertainty over when heavy AI investments will translate into profits. Meanwhile, South Korea’s tech-heavy market plunged over 6% on Tuesday as the selloff in AI-linked stocks deepened.IT stocks outlookVK Vijayakumar, chief investment strategist at Geojit Investments, said strong results from major IT companies and positive management commentary had triggered a sharp recovery in the IT index, helping the Nifty remain resilient. He added that the improvement could provide fundamental support to the broader market.Axis Securities however remains cautiously optimistic about the IT services sector. For the Indian IT sector, the pace of global AI adoption over the next 2-3 years remains a key concern for earnings growth and valuations.Also read: New CAS rules decoded: What Sebi’s revised framework means for stock market traders However, if questions arise globally around the commercial viability of AI, potentially slowing its rollout, market concerns over Indian IT companies could ease, said Krishna Sanghavi, CIO Equity, Mahindra Manulife Mutual Fund. The sector may remain positive in the near term, supported by improving sentiment and buying interest following HCLTech's results, but after a sharp rally, some profit-booking and volatility cannot be ruled out, said Gaurav Garg, head of research at Lemonn Market desk.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Veer Sharma, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. item.title: Rupee relief comes with disruptions in financial markets
item.description: The Reserve Bank of India took decisive steps to stabilize the rupee, significantly affecting financial markets. New constraints led to skyrocketing hedging costs and dwindled liquidity in the forex sector. Moreover, bond yields soared to their highest in three years due to escalating oil prices and foreign outflows. Banks brace for possible downturns and reduced foreign-exchange dealings in the next quarter.
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: The Reserve Bank of India’s historic defense of the rupee bought the currency some reprieve, but at a steep cost.The rupee is set for a 1.9% advance this week, its biggest weekly gain in four years. Yet liquidity in parts of the foreign-exchange market is drying up, hedging costs have jumped to a decade-high and bond yields have reached their highest level in more than three years.134985562The RBI’s most aggressive currency intervention in more than a decade is rippling across India’s financial markets. Tighter restrictions have disrupted most of the hedging activity that typically helps absorb currency shocks, while sowing confusion as traders pressed the central bank to ease the rules and clarify their scope.“Hedging costs shooting higher and illiquid markets are the unintended consequences,” said Anshul Chandak, head of treasury at RBL Bank in Mumbai. “We will have to swallow poison for a long-term gain.”Hedging CostsHedging has become more expensive because the RBI’s restrictions raised the cost of using derivatives — contracts linked to an underlying asset or price, such as the dollar-rupee exchange rate. Banks and companies use currency forwards and swaps to protect themselves against the risk that future dollar payments become more expensive.The measures, unveiled on Saturday, ordered lenders to set aside 20% of the rupee equivalent of foreign-exchange derivative transactions exceeding $2 million.Yields on onshore dollar-rupee forwards, a measure of the cost of securing dollars for future delivery, have surged. The three-month yield climbed to 6.54% on Thursday, its highest close since May 2016.The forwards market has become “extremely dislocated,” said Abhishek Goenka, chief executive officer of IFA Global, a forex advisory firm. It is now cheaper for companies to borrow rupees and swap them into dollars than to borrow the US currency, he said.Trading volumes have also fallen sharply, prompting Goenka to advise clients to hedge only their immediate needs.Bonds have also taken a hit. Elevated oil prices and foreign outflows are fueling bets that the RBI may have to rely more on interest-rate hikes if currency intervention alone fails to contain pressure on the rupee.The RBI sought to clear up some of the confusion on Thursday, saying the new rules would apply only to transactions used to hedge foreign-exchange risk and not to trades banks conduct to buy and sell currencies for clients and keep the market functioning.Banks are nevertheless bracing for the fallout. Treasury desks will likely see subdued client foreign-exchange business and potential losses on their fixed-income trading books in the October-December quarter, RBL’s Chandak said.Should liquidity remain thin and hedging costs stay elevated, companies and investors may demand higher returns to hold rupee assets — or become more reluctant to increase their exposure. That could leave the currency more vulnerable when the RBI eventually scales back its support.Investors will be watching the RBI’s future moves closely because predictability is critical, according to Shamaila Khan, head of global emerging markets and Asia-Pacific fixed income at UBS Asset Management.“The key is maintaining a transparent framework and efficient ability to hedge and transact,” Khan said. The measures haven’t materially altered UBS’s strategic view of India or its allocation to the country, but higher hedging costs will increase the returns it demands from Indian assets, she added.
